question.leadin: This ruler founded the Achaemenid [ah-KEE-men-id] Empire, which successfully grew by supporting local rulers as satraps and respecting local customs.
question.text: Name this "Great" Persian ruler of the sixth century BCE who ended the Babylonian Captivity.
question.clue: This victor of the Battle of Thymbra passed the Edict of Restoration, which granted the Jews religious tolerance, ending the Babylonian Captivity.

swap.text: In the Battles of Issus and Gaugamela, Alexander defeated Darius III, the ruler of this large empire centered on modern-day Iran.
swap.answerHtml: the First Persian Empire [or the Achaemenid Empire, or Xšāça]
swap.clue: King Psamtik III was defeated at the battle of Pelesium near the Nile Delta by a ruler of this empire named Cambyses II.

question.text: On Carter's last day in office, the signing of the Algiers Accords ended an event in this country. During that "hostage crisis" in this country, supporters of Ayatollah Khomeini invaded its U.S. embassy.
question.answerHtml: Iran [or Persia or Islamic Republic of Iran or IRI or Jomhuri-ye Eslâmi-ye Irân]
question.clue: 52 Americans were taken hostage in this country's capital during a "hostage crisis."

swap.leadin: Just decades after the Message of Muhammad, the Caliphate defeated two of the greatest empires in the world.
swap.text: Name this Persian Empire that was decisively beaten at the Battle of the Chains, al-Qadisiyah, and Nahavand. This dynasty succeeded the Parthians, although the exact circumstances are still unclear.
swap.clue: This empire was defeated at Qadisiyyah at the hands of Umar's general, Khalid ibn al-Walid.

question.text: The tyrant Aristagoras of Miletus led the Ionian Revolt against this ruler. The thirty-six satraps were established by this Persian ruler, whose forces invading Greece were defeated at Marathon.
question.clue: After his predecessor died of gangrene, this king and six other nobles assassinated a magician pretending to be Bardiya named Gaumata, an event described in his cliff-face Behistun Inscription.

swap.text: The defenders of Edessa hung a squealing pig to frighten away an elephant used by this empire's Khosrau I (KUZ-rao the first). This longest-lasting Persian dynasty rivaled the Byzantines in the Middle East.
swap.answerHtml: Sassanian Empire [or Sassanid Empire; or Sassanian Dynasty; or Sassanid Dynasty; or Eranshahr]
swap.clue: The Byzantines fought a series of wars with this empire. Shapur the Great was one ruler of this empire. It was the final, non-Islamic dynasty to rule over all of Persia.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about the Roman defeat at the Battle of Carrhae.
question.text: This Iranian empire defeated Rome at the Battle of Carrhae. They won the battle partially through the use of their namesake "shot," which involved horse archers firing behind them while retreating.
question.clue: At one battle, a general of this empire ordered his soldiers to cover their horses with cloth, thereby disguising the gleam of their armor.

swap.text: According to the Chronicle of Early Kings, Sargon defeated an attempted invasion by four "great" generals from this polity, which was led by the King of Awan.
swap.clue: The "Lament for Ur" describes a conquest by these people, whose Shutrukid dynasty later defeated the Kassites and looted the stele bearing the Code of Hammurabi from Babylon.

question.leadin: Identify the following about the history of measuring years.
question.text: The minyan shətarot ("meen-YAHN shuh-tah-ROHT") dating system used by Yemenite Jews is based on this ruler's reconquest of Babylon. In the contemporary dating system, this ruler was assassinated by Ptolemy Ceraunus in 281 BCE.
question.answerHtml: Seleucus I Nicator [or Seleucus the Victorious; or Seleucus Nicator; or Séleukos Nikátōr; prompt on Seleucus]
question.clue: He dispatched the ambassador Megasthenes on expeditions to the east, resulting in the production of theIndika.

swap.text: This non-Persian empire of Iran was conquered by Cyrus the Great before he went on to conquer Lydia and Babylon, aided by a defector from this empire, Harpagus. Its last king was Astyages and its capital was Ecbatana.
swap.clue: As a result of a battle at the Halys River, that waterway was declared its border with Lydia.

question.text: The victors at Carhae were an army of this empire founded by Arsaces I, which ruled in from the third century BCE to the third century CE before Ardashir I overthrew them and established the Sassanian empire.

swap.leadin: One account says this ruler died while fighting Queen Tomyris and her Massagetae people.
swap.text: Name this ruler, whose son and successor was Cambyses II. He defeated the Babylonians at the battle of Opis and his Edict of Restoration ended the Israelites' Babylonian captivity.
swap.answerHtml: Cyrus II [accept Cyrus the Great or Cyrus the Elder]
swap.clue: This man defeated Nabonidus at the Battle of the Opis and bested Croesus at the Battle of Thymbra to conquer the Lydian Empire.

question.text: The Masoretic text includes notes in this language, which is also used for most of the Kaddish prayer. Jesus primarily spoke this language.
question.clue: Demons found in the Ginza Rabba were repelled using ceramic bowls with incantations in this language.

swap.text: The Royal Road allowed these provincial governors to rapidly receive orders from Susa, as Artaphernes had during the Ionian Revolt. Several Indo-Scythian or Saka rulers were known as the "western" branches of these governors.
swap.answerHtml: satraps [accept satrapy or satrapies; accept khshathrapa or khshathrapavan or kshetrapal; accept Western Satraps or Great Satraps or Mahakṣatrapa; prompt on client kings or vassals or viceroys or archons]
swap.clue: 26 positions with this title were established around 580 BCE, a number that later increased to 36 according to the Behistun Inscription.

question.leadin: After being deposed, Khosrow II of this dynasty regained his throne with the help of the Byzantine Emperor Maurice, but later invaded the Byzantine Empire after Maurice was himself usurped by Phocas.
question.text: Name this last pre-Islamic Persian dynasty, which unsuccessfully besieged Constantinople in 626.
question.clue: A university at Gondishapur that was established by this Persian dynasty contained an advanced hospital that gave accreditation to local physicians. This dynasty was founded by Ardashir and included rulers like Shapur.

swap.leadin: Robert Haug argued that this empire's defeat formed a "shatterzone" where Arabs initially raided Hephthalites and Sogdians rather than "conquering" Tukharistan and Transoxiana.
swap.text: Name this empire that fell after the Battle of Nahavand in 642. Haug disputed al-Tabari's report that its last shah, Yazdegerd III, fled to Khorasan.
swap.answerHtml: Sasanian Empire [or Sassanid Empire, Sasanians, Sassanids, Sasan, or Ērānšahr; prompt on Neo-Persian Empire or New Persian Empire or Iranian Empire] (Haug wrote The Eastern Frontier: Limits of Empire in Late Antique and Early Medieval Central Asia.)
swap.clue: The main feature remaining from this empire's capital is the Taq Kasra brickwork vault.

question.text: According to classical sources, the Kingdom of Urartu's capital of Tushpa fell to these people under Cyaxares in 590 BC. Herodotus described seven concentric walls surrounding this kingdom's mountain capital of Ecbatana.
question.answerHtml: Medes [or the Median Empire or Median Kingdom or Kingdom of Media; accept Māda or Mādāya]
question.clue: Early kings of these people included Deioces and Phraortes.

swap.leadin: What is called the "largest Greek structure built in India" is thought to be a temple to this religion built by an offshoot of the House of Suren.
swap.text: Name this chief religion sponsored by the Indo-Parthians and Parthians. Today, practitioners of this religion in India are called Parsees.
swap.answerHtml: Zoroastrianism [or word forms, or Mazdaism or word forms]
swap.clue: The Sassanids proselytized this state religion of theirs, though it did not spread as far as Manichaeism or Christianity. This religion venerates Ahura Mazda.

question.leadin: Answer these questions about Alexander the Great's return from India, FTPE.
question.text: Upon arriving in Susa, Alexander found that this treasurer had taken large quantities of money and soldiers and bolted town for Athens. This man was eventually killed in Crete.
question.clue: This general had to eat his own son after Astyages discovered he did not actually murder an infant prophesied to overthrow him. He would later understandably mutiny against Astyages at the Battle of Pasargadae.

swap.text: This son of Kavahd didn't care much for Mazdak or his sect and ousted them. This ruler is likely the most renowned Sassanid king and warred with Justinian after concluding the Eternal Peace with him. His grandson, the second ruler of his name, was busted up by Heraclius.
swap.answerHtml: Chosroes I (or Khosrau or Khusrav or Khosrow or Osroes or Husrev)
swap.clue: Justinian's main rival throughout his reign was this Sassanid Emperor, who prosecuted the Lazic War and defeated the Bactrians and the Hephthalite Empire during his rule from 531-579 AD.
